entry.title: Every redesign is an information architecture project

link.title: Every redesign is an information architecture project

entry.content:
This sounds like an overstatement until you look at what actually happens. You cut a section. You decide not to build a page because something elsewhere already covers it. You leave a body of content on another team’s platform and link to it instead. Each of those changes what a reader can find and how they find it. Each one is an architectural decision.

The decisions get made either way. The only variable is whether you make them deliberately, or inherit them from whatever the old structure happened to do.

Here are seven questions a redesign will ask you. You don’t get to skip any of them. You only get to choose whether you answer them on purpose.

1. Boundaries: what belongs here at all

Before you decide how content is structured, decide what content is in scope.

Most redesigns treat this as settled. The assumption is that the boundary of the space is the boundary of what’s in it today. That assumption is almost always wrong, because the current contents are a record of what previous teams happened to publish, not a considered decision about what belongs.

On one project, a large body of enablement material lived on a separate platform owned by another team. The question wasn’t whether that content was good. It was whether it belonged inside our information space, adjacent to it, or linked from it. Three different answers, three different architectures.

A related question came up with frequently asked questions. The obvious move was to build a FAQ section. The decision was not to, because a community forum already served that need and served it better. That’s a boundary drawn on purpose rather than by omission.

Ask early: what are the neighbouring content systems, who owns them, and where does the edge sit?

2. Inventory: what you actually have

You can’t restructure what you haven’t enumerated.

This is the least interesting step and reliably the longest. It’s also the one teams skip, because the navigation looks like an inventory. It isn’t. Navigation is a map of what someone once believed existed, maintained by people who had other priorities.

A real inventory turns up three things you didn’t expect. Content that exists but is unreachable. Content that’s reachable by two different paths that disagree with each other. And content that everyone assumed existed and doesn’t.

When we audited coverage against the actual feature set rather than the existing content list, the gap was much larger than the number everyone had been quoting. Neither number was dishonest. They were measured against different denominators, and nobody had examined the denominator.

Do the inventory first. Expect it to take longer than the restructuring that follows.

3. Grouping: how things nest

This is the part people mean when they say information architecture. It’s the visible output: categories, hierarchy, depth.

The recurring failure is grouping content the way the product is built rather than the way people look for it. Internal structure is seductive because it’s already agreed, already documented, and matches how teams are organised. It’s also invisible to the reader, who arrives with a task rather than an org chart.

When the two conflict, the reader’s model wins. That’s uncomfortable, because defending it means telling colleagues their team’s shape isn’t going to show up in the navigation.

4. Labels: what you call things

Naming is architecture, not copy.

A perfect hierarchy with internal names is unfindable. The gap between what a team calls a feature and what a reader calls it is where most searches fail, and it rarely closes on its own, because the internal term is the one everyone in the room already uses.

Part of our redesign involved reopening a feature’s name. The internal term was accurate and well established. It wasn’t the term readers typed. Renaming was harder than restructuring, and mattered more.

Test your labels with people who don’t work on the product. If a name needs explaining, it isn’t doing its job.

5. Entry points: how people arrive

Almost nobody arrives at your homepage.

People land in the middle of your structure: from a search engine, a support reply, a link inside the product, a colleague’s message. A hierarchy that only makes sense when read from the top is broken for most of the traffic it receives.

Instead of designing the landing page, we mapped every entry point for each type of content: where a reader could arrive from, and what they would see when they got there. The exercise changed the design, because several routes led to pages that made no sense without context the reader didn’t have.

Every page is a landing page. Structure has to survive being entered in the middle.

6. Access: who can see what

This one gets treated as a permissions detail to settle after launch. It’s structure.

If parts of your space are visible only to some readers, you don’t have one architecture. You have several overlapping ones, and each reader experiences a different shape. That’s manageable, but only if you design it rather than discover it.

There are usually three states, not two. Public. Restricted behind a sign-in. And a third, awkward category: technically reachable by anyone with a link, but never intended for a general audience. We found content in that third state which was entirely appropriate for the audience it was built for, and a problem the moment the surrounding space became public.

Label every item by visibility during the inventory. The third state is the one that causes trouble.

7. Lifecycle: what happens to what you replace

Redesigns create orphans: superseded pages, dead links, articles that now say something the product no longer does.

For each replaced item, there are three options. Redirect it to whatever supersedes it. Archive it so it stays available but stops being promoted. Or remove it. Choosing nothing means choosing the fourth option, which is leaving it in place to contradict the new content.

There’s an opportunity here worth naming. Nobody deprecates documentation voluntarily: there’s no reward for it and there’s always something more pressing. A redesign is usually the only moment an organisation will agree to clean up. Use the cover while you have it.

The default is still an answer

None of these questions are optional. A redesign that ignores boundaries inherits them. A redesign that skips the inventory restructures a subset of what exists and calls it complete. A redesign that treats access as a permissions task ships a structure that behaves differently for different readers, and finds out later.

The work isn’t adding an information architecture phase to your project. It’s recognising that you’re already doing the work, and deciding to do it deliberately.

entry.title: How to write docs for agents

link.title: How to write docs for agents

entry.content:
Somewhere in the last year, our audience quietly changed. It’s not just people opening our docs anymore, it’s agents. Claude Code answering a question by fetching a page. A RAG pipeline pulling one paragraph out of context. A support bot summarizing a policy doc in half a second. If your writing only makes sense to a human reading top to bottom, an agent grabbing one chunk out of order won’t get it.

Here’s what actually changes when you write for that reader too.

Hot tips for writing docs agents can actually use

  • Make every section stand alone. Agents often retrieve one chunk, not the whole page. “As discussed above” means nothing to something that never saw “above.”
  • Front-load the answer. Skip the warm-up paragraph. Say the fact in sentence one.
  • Use descriptive links, not “click here.” An agent following a link needs the link text to be the description.
  • Reach for structure over prose. Tables, steps, code blocks: agents pattern-match structure far more reliably than they parse dense paragraphs for the same fact.
  • Cut the marketing language. “Seamlessly,” “powerful,” “game-changing” is noise an agent has to filter past to find the actual fact.
  • Publish a manifest, not just pages. Formats like llms.txt give agents an explicit index instead of making them infer structure by crawling. You can check out the llms.txt directory to see what a good one looks like.

How I actually found this out

I stumbled onto this looking into llms.txt, a format sites now publish specifically so agents can read them efficiently. Reading the spec, I went and checked my own site to see how far behind I was.

I wasn’t behind. I already had a feed.xml, a sitemap.xml, and structured metadata on every page: a clean, structured list of everything I’ve published, no rendering or guessing required. I’d set all of it up months ago for SEO and so RSS readers could subscribe to my posts. I never once thought about agents when I did it. Turns out a feed reader and an agent want the exact same thing: a plain list of what exists, not a page they have to parse to figure it out. llms.txt is solving a problem RSS solved decades ago. I already had the fix running in the background.

So I went further and pulled up my blog’s quality checker, a script I run before every post goes live. One rule jumped out immediately: descriptive link text, not “click here” or “read more.” I’d built that in July, purely so human readers wouldn’t hit a vague link and bounce. Not one thought about agents.

Then I checked the rest of the checker. Almost every rule held up the same way. One H1 per post, no skipped heading levels: added so my posts wouldn’t ramble, and it also means anything reading my headings gets a clean outline instead of guessing structure from font size. Alt text required on every image: added for accessibility, and it’s the only way a text-only reader knows what the image even shows. A filler-phrase check flagging things like “it is important to note”: added to tighten my prose, and it has the exact same effect as cutting noise for a reader that’s scanning for the fact, not the flourish.

I never designed a single one of these for agents. I designed all of them so a human wouldn’t roll their eyes and close the tab. Writing clearly for people was never really a different skill from writing clearly for machines. We just didn’t know we needed to check.

entry.title: Agentic automation for technical writers: where to start

link.title: Agentic automation for technical writers: where to start

entry.content:
Every technical writer has a moment where they think, “didn’t I just do this exact thing last week?” Formatting checks before every publish, hunting down broken links after every release, confirming which articles reference a term that just changed. None of it is hard, it’s just the same motion, over and over, and it quietly eats the hours you meant to spend actually writing.

The good news: most of these moments are automatable. The hard part isn’t the tooling, it’s knowing which task is worth automating in the first place.

How to spot the task worth automating

Before you build anything, run the task through three questions:

  1. Frequency, How many times have I done this exact thing this month?
  2. Pattern, Is the input and output basically the same shape every time?
  3. Effort vs. value, Does doing this manually cost me more time than automating it would, over a few cycles?

If a task clears all three, it’s not a “nice to have” automation, it’s a task quietly asking to be fixed.

A knowledge base is code too

A knowledge base isn’t just a pile of articles, it’s a system, the same way a codebase is one. Articles depend on each other, reference the same features, break when something upstream changes, and go stale if nobody’s watching. Once you see it that way, automation stops feeling like an engineering thing bolted onto writing, and starts feeling like ordinary maintenance, the same reason engineers automate builds, tests, and cleanup for their codebase.

Take release week, for me. Every cycle, I ran the same loop: check which existing articles might be affected by the change, open each candidate, re-read it, and confirm whether it needed an update. Across dozens of articles, under release-week time pressure, that added up fast, every single cycle.

Run it through the three questions: same task every release (frequency), same shape each time, search, open, read, judge (pattern), and the manual version was costing more focused hours than a fix would (effort vs. value). Clear yes on all three. So instead of manually searching and rereading, I built a small custom MCP for it, I just open the Claude Code terminal, describe what changed, and it surfaces the articles actually relevant to that change, so I can confirm relevance in a fraction of the time instead of re-reading a dozen articles to rule out ten of them.

Where automation shows up for TWs

A few categories worth knowing, even if you never touch all of them:

  • Publishing, build/deploy pipelines that turn your Markdown into a live site automatically (more on this in a future post)
  • Quality checks, prose linting, broken-link checks, running automatically before anything ships
  • Content generation, turning demo or webinar transcripts into a first-draft help article instead of writing one from a blank page
  • Maintenance, flagging content that’s gone stale or hasn’t been touched in months

Start smaller than you think

The temptation once you see this pattern is to automate everything at once. Don’t. Pick the one task that keeps showing up and costing you real time, fix that first, and let the next automation reveal itself the same way this one did, by being annoying enough, often enough, to notice.

entry.title: Meet Ciara, my personal assistant(agent)
entry.content:
No, I did not get one.

Ciara is my work log agent I set up to track everything I work on during the week, synthesise it, and drop it into my notes every Friday. Named her, gave her instructions, connected her to my tools. She’s not a person but she does the one thing I’ve never managed to do consistently myself: keep a clear record of what I actually did.

I’ve been using her for the past few weeks now, and honestly, it’s so easy. Here’s why I built her, and how.

Do you actually know what you did last week?

Most people don’t.

Not because they weren’t working, but because knowledge work leaves no obvious trail. You finish a doc, close a tab, move to the next thing. By Friday, the week is a blur. By the following Tuesday, it’s gone.

And then someone asks you something.

“Hey, what was the status of that API doc we discussed?” “Did we ever resolve that comment from the engineering team?”

And you know you dealt with it. You just can’t remember where, or when, or what you concluded. So you start digging: Slack, email, your CMS, Jira, calendar, triangulating your own past from six different systems that don’t talk to each other.

That’s a lot of effort just to answer a question about your own work.

The problem isn’t recall. It’s collation.

Your work is documented. It’s just documented in fragments, scattered across every tool you touch. There’s no single place that says: here is what you did this week, in plain language, in one place.

This is the gap Ciara fills.

How I built her

Ciara runs on Claude Code, connected to the tools where my work actually lives:

  • Google Workspace, Calendar, Gmail, and Drive (pre-built MCP integrations, took minutes to set up)
  • Slack (same, pre-built connector, a few config steps)
  • My CMS, I built a custom MCP connector for our documentation portal, since it doesn’t have a public one. It gives Ciara read access to my published docs, drafts, and revision history

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is the standard that lets an AI agent connect to external tools, think of it as the plumbing that lets Ciara read your actual data, not just chat with you about it.

The second piece is her instruction file, a plain text README that lives in my Claude Code project. It tells Ciara exactly what to do:

  • Where to look: calendar events I organised or attended, Slack threads I replied in, docs I created or revised, emails where I was the primary sender or decision-maker
  • What to skip: FYI threads, automated notifications, calendar holds
  • How to group it: by project, not by tool, and flag anything still open
  • What format I want: one short paragraph at the top, then bullets by project, then a “still in progress” list at the bottom

That instruction file is the real work. The more precisely you describe what counts as meaningful output versus background noise, the better Ciara’s summaries get. I treat it like briefing a new team member: specific, no assumptions, updated when my workflow changes.

What changes

The next time someone asks me something, in a meeting, on Slack, mid-conversation, I don’t have to excavate. I open my notes, find the relevant week, and I have the answer in under a minute.

More useful than that: I stop losing track of my own work. A lot of the cognitive overhead of knowledge work isn’t the work itself, it’s the ongoing effort of remembering what you did, where things stand, and what’s still waiting on you. One clear record per week removes most of that.

Where to start

If you have Google Workspace and Slack, you can have a basic version of Ciara running today, both have pre-built MCP connectors for Claude Code. Write a simple instruction file, run it at the end of the week, save the output somewhere you’ll actually check.

If your most important tool is something custom, a CMS, an internal wiki, a proprietary ticketing system, check if it has an API. If it does, you can build a connector. It’s less work than it sounds.

Every Friday, I ask Ciara what I got done. She tells me. It takes about few minutes, and I haven’t once had to dig through six tools to answer a question about my own work since.

She’s not a person. But she’s a pretty good assistant.

Monisha

entry.title: The data technical writers should be paying attention to

link.title: The data technical writers should be paying attention to

entry.content:
Documentation impact has always been hard to quantify, but the data to prove it exists. You just need to know where to look and what it is connected to. Here are the metrics worth tracking, and why each one matters beyond the docs team.

Failed searches, your backlog already written

Every failed search is a user who came to your portal, typed a real question, and left without an answer. It is a timestamped documentation gap, no guessing required. When customers can not find answers, they contact support or a CSM. That is a measurable cost. Reducing failed searches is one of the clearest ways to connect documentation work to support deflection.

Search-to-view conversion, the findability check

Good docs that no one can find have no value. This metric tells you whether your content surfaces when users go looking for it. Track it monthly and it becomes a trend: “conversion improved from 70% to 76%” tells leadership that self-service is improving and CSM capacity is being protected.

Article drop-off, where the journey ends

Drop-off shows you where users stop reading mid-article. High drop-off midway through a procedure usually means the doc is incomplete or unclear, and users who hit a wall do not wait, they contact support. This metric separates docs that exist from docs that actually work.

Coverage completeness, the go-live lens

A doc existing is not the same as a user being able to complete a task. Track coverage (does a doc exist?) and completeness (does it take the user all the way through?) separately, and connect both to implementation timelines. Gaps here are go-live risks, they surface post-launch as escalations, not internal reporting misses.

Communication metrics, how your content actually lands

Release notes and documentation emails have their own data layer: open rate, click-through rate, deliverability. Together they form a funnel, sent to delivered to opened to clicked. A drop anywhere has a specific cause. Customers who do not read release notes miss feature updates, which leads to underutilisation and reactive support calls. Treat these numbers the way a marketing team treats campaign metrics.

Workload and blocked status, team health as a delivery signal

A backlog growing faster than the team can clear means coverage gaps are accumulating. Blocked tickets mean work is sitting, and if a doc is blocked when a feature ships, that is an implementation readiness problem, not just a process issue. Velocity reported upward makes the case for capacity and planning investment before it becomes a crisis.

Every metric here connects to something leadership already measures: support cost, self-service capability, feature adoption, implementation readiness, customer engagement, delivery risk. The data is almost always already being collected. The job is to bring it together and use it to make decisions.

That is what turns a documentation team into a documentation strategy.

Next up: how I built a live dashboard to track all of this, and what the data revealed once everything was in one place.

entry.title: “It shouldn’t take that long”: what’s really happening on our end

link.title: “It shouldn’t take that long”: what’s really happening on our end

entry.content:
We’re hearing this one a lot more lately. And I think I know why.

Stakeholders have started handing us their own documents (AI-generated write-ups, screenshots included) and saying, essentially, “here you go.” And sure, if the job were to take that document and hit Publish, they’d be right. It wouldn’t take long at all. But publishing is where our job begins, not ends.

Step one: verifying the flow

The first thing I do with any handoff, human-written or AI-generated, is replicate the flow myself. I open the product, I follow the steps, and almost every time, the sequential order in the document doesn’t match what actually happens on screen. The feature behaves differently than described. A step is missing. Two steps are in the wrong order.

And the AI-generated version? Oh, it’s thorough. It has a Definition section. It has a Key Benefits section (I know). It has an Executive Summary explaining what the feature does in three confident, beautifully structured paragraphs.

What it doesn’t have is accuracy. AI doesn’t hallucinate quietly. It hallucinates in complete sentences with excellent grammar. Which means I’m not just editing for style. I’m fact-checking every claim against the live product, hunting for the places where the prose sounds right but the information is wrong.

Step two: structure doesn’t exist yet, and that’s my job

What I receive is text. What users need is a document.

That gap, between text and document, is invisible to everyone but me. It’s where I decide: does this need a table or a list? Where do headings go, and what should they say? How do I categorize this information so that the person who needs step 4 doesn’t have to read steps 1 through 3 to find it?

These aren’t cosmetic decisions. They’re architectural. And they have to be consistent, not just internally within this doc, but across every other document we’ve published. Readers notice when one doc calls it “Prerequisites” and another calls it “Before You Begin” and a third just buries the requirements in paragraph two without a heading at all.

I’m the one making sure that doesn’t happen.

Step three: the screenshots are a whole thing

Let’s talk about the screenshots, because this one deserves its own section.

Every screenshot goes through a verification pass: does it contain real user data, real email addresses, real names, anything that should not be published on a documentation site?

And while I’m doing that, I’m also checking something else entirely: is this screenshot even current? Documentation gets written at a point in time. The UI doesn’t stay still. A button that was labeled “Submit” in the screenshot might now say “Save and Continue.” A field that lived on screen two might have moved to screen three in the last release. The text in the document still references the old label, so now I’m not just swapping out screenshots. I’m tracking down every place in the content where that UI label appears and updating those too.

And then, mid-review, a Slack ping arrives: “Hey, just so you know, that feature no longer exists. We changed it to XYZ.”

So now I’m not just updating a screenshot. I’m going back through the entire document to find every place this feature was mentioned, every step that referenced it, every heading built around it, and reworking all of it to reflect the update.

Then, after the PII check and the currency check: do we even need this many screenshots? There’s a threshold where a doc stops being helpful and starts being a scroll-through experience with captions. Knowing where that line is comes from exposure to real readers, and that judgment is mine to make.

The work that lives between the steps

There’s the translation work: taking what stakeholders know deeply, what they want to say, and what users actually need, and finding the sentence that serves all three without lying to any of them.

And there’s the governance work: making sure this new doc doesn’t contradict the three existing docs about the same topic, that the terminology is consistent, and that the screenshots don’t show a UI that was deprecated in Q2.

None of this appears in the final document. Which means none of it is legible to the people saying “it shouldn’t take that long.”

A tool can produce text. A technical writer produces documentation.

And documentation takes exactly as long as it takes.

entry.title: AI needs me as much as I need AI

link.title: AI needs me as much as I need AI

entry.content:
I use AI for almost everything I do now. And somewhere along the way, I stopped thinking of it as something that might replace me, and started thinking of it as something that genuinely needs me.

Not in a motivational-poster kind of way. In a literal, functional way.

AI runs on human knowledge

At its core, AI is trained on data. But here’s the thing: a human created all of it. Every document, every wiki, every API reference, every support thread: that’s the raw material AI learns from. It doesn’t generate knowledge. It processes knowledge that already exists.

And that knowledge comes from people who work: writers, engineers, product managers, marketers, anyone who has ever documented something or explained something to someone else.

AI is only as good as the knowledge it was trained on. And humans built all of it.

Without structure, AI is just noise

Recently, I was doing research for a project. I asked AI to research for me without giving it any real direction: no structure, no focus, no sense of what I was looking for or how I wanted things to connect.

The output was overwhelming. A lot of information, none of it making sense together. I didn’t even know where to start with it.

Then I went back and defined exactly what I needed: the structure, the focus, how I wanted the findings to connect. The results after that were genuinely useful, though I still had to tweak and shape them.

If I had just set up a research agent and let it run blind, it would have produced noise forever. The human has to define the problem before AI can help solve it.

The knowledge quality problem

Here’s something that doesn’t get talked about enough: AI is only as reliable as the knowledge it’s working from.

My team recently used an agent to generate documentation from internal resources. When we sent the docs for review, some of them were outdated, even though the agent had referenced the actual codebase. It took a human reviewer to catch it.

The agent did exactly what it was asked to do. But it had no way of knowing that certain information was stale. No way of applying judgment about what was still true versus what had quietly changed.

Even with a quality-check agent, someone has to set the validation rules. And someone has to decide what “correct” looks like. That’s not something you can automate away.

AI agents do the work you ask them to do

The promise of AI agents is real, and they can take on significant chunks of work autonomously. But they are still doing the work you ask them to do.

You define what the agent knows. You define what it’s allowed to do. You decide what judgment calls it cannot make on its own. You catch it when it goes wrong.

That’s not a workaround. That’s the design.

The relationship is mutual

I need AI. It makes me faster and sharper. But AI needs me to provide the knowledge it learns from, give it the right context, direct it toward the right problem, and apply the judgment it cannot.

As AI takes on more work, the humans who know how to direct it well become more valuable, not less. The knowledge systems that power AI don’t build themselves. The agents that automate work don’t design themselves.

They need us. They always will.

These are my personal thoughts after a decade in documentation and now working alongside AI every day. Next, I’ll be writing about what it means to write for AI systems, and why it’s becoming one of the most important skills in the field.

Monisha

entry.title: Technical writers in the age of AI: we’re not done, we’re just getting started

link.title: Technical writers in the age of AI: we’re not done, we’re just getting started

entry.content:
I’ll be honest with you. When the AI wave started hitting, I was scared.

I’ve been a technical writer for over a decade. Suddenly, everyone was saying: “Hey, AI writes really well now. Isn’t that basically your job?” I started noticing engineers and product managers writing their own documents, then just sending them to me for a quick review. And I thought: even that’s going to stop soon.

That fear was real. But here’s what happened: the better AI got, the more clearly I could see what it couldn’t do.

Technical writing was never just writing

This is what I had to learn, and honestly, it took AI to teach it to me.

For years, I thought my job was about crafting the right sentences, making complex things readable. But that was never the core of it.

The core was always the decision-making behind the writing.

Why does this document need to exist? Who is going to read it, and in what state of panic or confusion? Which warning saves a user from a 3am support call? AI can generate a thousand words in seconds. It cannot answer any of those questions.

After years of sitting in cross-functional meetings, watching how documentation actually gets used, I carry institutional knowledge no model has access to. I know why we don’t structure things a certain way, because we tried it two years ago and it created a flood of tickets. I know what our users panic about at midnight. That’s not writing. That’s judgment.

Where AI actually helps and where it doesn’t

I use AI heavily in my work, and I want to be clear: I’m not anti-AI. I’m pro-knowing-what-you’re-doing.

AI is an incredible tool if you already know what you’re doing. If you have the experience, the context, the relationships, AI becomes a multiplier. It handles the mechanical first draft, sets up automations that previously ate up hours, and cuts repetitive formatting work. The result? I spend more time on strategy and identifying gaps, and less time on things that were never what made my role valuable.

But here’s the flip side.

If you depend on AI without the underlying experience, you’re in trouble. Not because AI will replace you, but because it will confidently produce work that looks right and isn’t. It’ll generate documentation that misses the point, structure content for the wrong audience, skip the warning that would have saved someone hours. And you won’t know, because you haven’t built the instincts to catch it.

AI doesn’t know your users. It doesn’t know your product’s history. It doesn’t know that one edge case your engineering team quietly fixed six months ago.

You need the experience to direct AI well. That experience doesn’t come from prompting.

The traditional TW role is changing, and that’s okay

If your current job looks like: get a knowledge transfer from engineering, convert it into a document, publish, maintain. That workflow will get automated. Parts of it already are.

That’s not the end. That’s the signal to evolve.

What makes a technical writer irreplaceable today:

  • Proactively identifying what the team needs before anyone asks
  • Running docs like a system: architecture, health, consistency
  • Identifying what can be automated using AI and actually building those automations
  • Writing for highly technical audiences: developers, engineers, and the systems they build

And that last point matters more than people realize. End users who once needed step-by-step UI guides? AI agents are increasingly handling that for them. The documentation that matters more and more is what developers, engineers, and AI systems themselves need: API references, architecture docs, agent-readable content. To write for them well, you need to understand how they think, how systems are structured, even the fundamentals of how code works.

So, will AI replace technical writers?

No. Not if you’re doing more than AI can do.

AI will replace the parts of the job that were always lower-value: the mechanical first draft, the rote formatting, the basic structure work.

What it can’t replace is the human who knows something is wrong before they can articulate why. Who has sat with users, navigated cross-functional dynamics, made judgment calls about what belongs where and why.

The floor of this job just got raised. And if you’re willing to rise with it, this is actually one of the best times to be a technical writer.

These are my personal thoughts after 10+ years in technical writing. Next, I’ll be exploring how AI needs knowledge to function and why technical writers are the ones who provide it.

— Monisha
